q: What mortality is associated with severe TBI?
why: Mild about 0.1%, moderate about 10%, severe about 40%.

q: Which is a primary brain injury?
why: Primary injuries happen at impact (fracture, contusion, haematoma, DAI); secondary injuries (oedema, ischaemia, hypoxia, hypotension) are what we prevent.

q: What PaO2 and PaCO2 are targeted in tier 1 TBI management?
why: Tier 1: PaO2 over 10 kPa, PaCO2 4.5–5 kPa, CPP 60–70 mmHg.

q: Which hypertonic saline dose is used for raised ICP in TBI (tier 2)?
why: Hypertonic saline (or 20% mannitol 0.5 g/kg) is a tier 2 option after repeat CT.

q: What does barbiturate coma for refractory ICP aim for on EEG?
why: Tier 3 options include decompressive craniectomy or barbiturate coma targeting about 50% burst suppression.

q: What is a recognised late complication of decompressive craniectomy?
o: Syndrome of the trephined or subdural hygroma
why: Delayed complications include infection, hydrocephalus, subdural hygroma and syndrome of the trephined.

q: Which level of transfer care applies to a ventilated patient with organ support?
why: Level 3 patients need advanced respiratory support or support of 2 or more organs.

q: Why is a metaraminol infusion useful during transfer?
o: It reduces the number of pumps and lines needed for BP support
why: Minimise pumps and secure access; metaraminol can be run peripherally.

q: What is the role of seizure prophylaxis after TBI?
o: Per local policy, early seizures are treated and prophylaxis is often given
why: Follow local policy; treat seizures promptly to reduce CMRO2 and ICP.
